text: This lab puts both of this chapter's mechanisms to work in one scenario: Acme's fleet application. An external dashboard needs to check a vehicle's status over REST without logging into the instance, and when a vehicle gets checked back in, several related records need updating in a way that's decoupled from whatever code detects the return.

Two requirements, two builds. First, a Scripted REST GET resource that answers a status check. Second, a Business Rule that announces a return event, and a Script Action that reacts to it independently.

The resource lives at slash vehicle slash sys_id slash status, GET. The script pulls the sys_id out of request dot path params, looks the vehicle up with the one-line veh dot get, and if nothing matches, answers with a 404 and an error body. If the vehicle is found, it also looks up that vehicle's most recent checkout record — ordering descending by creation date and limiting to one row — and assembles everything into a plain object handed to response dot set body.

On the trigger side, a Business Rule runs after update, with a condition of status changes to Returned. Its script does one thing only: it calls gs dot event queue with the event name vehicle dot returned, the current record, the vehicle's sys_id, and the returning user's sys_id as extra parameters. Notice what it does NOT do — it never touches the vehicle record directly.

A Script Action named Update Vehicle on Return listens for that same event name. Inside it, event dot parm1 and event dot parm2 hold the two extra values the Business Rule passed in. The script looks up the vehicle by that sys_id and, if found, sets its status back to available with a fresh last-returned timestamp.

Why split it this way instead of having the Business Rule update the vehicle directly? Because if a second team later needs their own reaction to the same return — an email alert, a sync to an external system — they add their own Script Action listening for vehicle dot returned, with zero changes to the Business Rule's code. That's loose coupling doing real work.

A working REST resource and a decoupled event reaction, built from the same GlideRecord patterns you've used all course. That wraps Chapter 8. Next up: Chapter 9 begins with Capstone Kickoff, Application Requirements — scoping the custom scoped application you'll build for the rest of this course.
